This scientific blog explores how BFS enhances digital agro-advisories, disaster preparedness, and real-time decision-making across sectors, positioning India as a leader in climate-smart governance and a contributor to Global South resilience. image created by author India has reached a groundbreaking milestone in meteorological science with the launch of the Bharat Forecast System (BFS), a next-generation weather prediction model that positions the country at the forefront of climate technology. Developed indigenously by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM) , Pune, and operationalized by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) , BFS is being lauded as the world’s first high-resolution weather model, offering forecasts at an unprecedented 6 km × 6 km spatial resolution. This transformative leap from IMD’s previous 12 km x 12 km resolution enhances the granularity of forecasts, reducing the unit of analysis from 144 sq km to just 36 sq km. Such refinement is critical for predicting localized weather events, like cloudbursts, flash floods, and extreme rainfall, that were previously difficult to track with broader-scale models. The Bharat Forecast System also benefits from satellite and remote sensing inputs provided by ISRO’s INSAT series, supporting data assimilation and improving forecast accuracy. The BFS has undergone rigorous testing since 2022, showing forecast accuracy improvements ranging from 30% to 64%, especially in core monsoon zones and for extreme rainfall events. The improvements in forecast accuracy are particularly notable in core monsoon zones and during extreme rainfall events. AI-Ready Infrastructure and High-Performance Computing Behind BFS BFS’s precision is powered by state-of-the-art high-performance computing. Initially tested on the Pratyush supercomputer (4.0 petaflops), the model’s real-time application required more speed. This demand was addressed by the inauguration of the Arka supercomputer at IITM in 2024, offering 11.77 petaflops of computing power and 33 petabytes of storage, enabling 10-day forecasts to be processed in just 3 to 4 hours, down from 10 to 12 hours. Built from scratch, the BFS model incorporates advanced numerical techniques like the Triangular Cubic Octahedral (TCO) grid, optimized for the Indian subcontinent’s unique meteorological dynamics. Additionally, the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) algorithms has enabled hyperlocal forecasts, a first for Indian meteorological models. Importantly, the BFS is designed to be AI-ready , with structured, scalable outputs that can integrate seamlessly into advanced analytics and decision-support systems across multiple sectors. This enables a diverse range of climate intelligence applications, such as predictive models, AI-powered agriculture advisories, urban flood forecasting, energy demand management, and automated early warning systems. These use cases benefit from the model’s ability to deliver granular, real-time weather data essential for informed decisions in agriculture, disaster risk reduction, public health, and infrastructure. Hyperlocal Precision for Local-Level Action With its 6-kilometer resolution, the BFS can deliver forecasts that reach down to the village level, transforming how India approaches localised weather services. Unlike the earlier 12 km x 12 km resolution, which covered larger administrative blocks, 6 km x 6 km grids reduce the area of analysis from 144 sq km to just 36 sq km. This allows BFS to identify specific weather changes such as thunderstorms, rainfall patterns, or dry spells within a much finer geographic range. This hyperlocal capability is crucial for: ● Urban governance , enabling village or neighbourhood-level alerts for heatwaves, lightning strikes, and urban flooding ● Disaster preparedness , supporting targeted evacuations or relief in flood-prone or cyclone-impacted areas ● Public health , by forecasting heatwaves or stagnant weather conditions that contribute to disease outbreaks ● Smart infrastructure planning , where localized weather inputs inform city drainage, traffic control, and construction scheduling ● Agriculture and rural livelihoods , by enabling village-level agro-advisories, improving timing of farm operations, and strengthening local preparedness for weather-related disruptions. These capabilities bring India closer to achieving a nationwide, decentralised early warning system that can operate at the level of villages and urban wards, making BFS an engine for localised risk reduction and adaptive action. Delivering Hyperlocal Agro-Advisories for Smallholder Empowerment BFS significantly transforms the farming community in India. By making weather forecasts more accurate for specific areas and times, it allows villages to predict rainfall, which helps create local farming advice. These hyperlocal forecasts support timely and resource-efficient decision-making across the entire cropping cycle: ● Sowing schedules and seed variety selection , aligned with rainfall onset and soil moisture conditions ● Irrigation and fertilization timing , based on anticipated dry spells or rainfall events, helping optimize water and nutrient use efficiency ● Pest and disease management , informed by humidity and temperature forecasts ● Harvest and post-harvest planning , reducing losses due to untimely rain or heat stress ● Market planning and logistics , through better predictability of harvest windows ● Contingency planning for extreme events like droughts, cyclones, or unseasonal rains. “A forecast at the right time is worth more than a field of advice” These hyperlocal forecasts are integrated into weekly agro-advisories disseminated through digital platforms such as Meghdoot , ICRISAT’s iSAT , mKisan , and a few other platforms. With the downscaled data from BFS, these platforms can now provide information that is specific to individual villages instead of just larger areas, making the advice more useful and relevant for farmers. Rather than replacing existing systems, BFS amplifies their value by enhancing precision, improving relevance, and enabling location-specific guidance across cropping stages. BFS now enables the targeting of villages with forecasts, improving upon current systems that previously issued advisories only at the block level. ● Decision confidence among farmers ● Input planning for agribusinesses ● Localised risk reduction AI models trained on hyperlocal forecasts can personalize advisories, tailoring them to crop types, stages, soil conditions, and local socioeconomic contexts. BFS thus acts as a critical data layer in building intelligent, farmer-facing platforms. Strengthening Real-Time Weather Response Systems with BFS Another key feature of BFS is Nowcasting, forecasting events for the next 2 hours, with aspirations to go as short as 10-minute forecasts for rapidly evolving events like thunderstorms. The system is enabled by India’s expanding Doppler radar network, which currently has 40 units with a target of 100 by 2026. It feeds real-time data into BFS for minute-by-minute updates. BFS enhances its services by fusing high-resolution forecasts with nowcast capabilities: ● Short-term agricultural advisories , such as immediate irrigation deferral or pest/disease alert or harvest pre-postponement ● Early warnings for floods, storms, and lightning , at the village level; ● Emergency response coordination , allowing authorities to act faster and more precisely; ● Last-mile alert systems , ensuring vulnerable communities receive timely, actionable warnings via SMS, apps, or local networks. Global Relevance and South-South Collaboration Potential Though designed for India, the Bharat Forecast System is optimized for tropical latitudes between 30°N and 30°S , making it suitable for use across much of the Global South , including Africa, Southeast Asia, and parts of Latin America . These regions face similar climate vulnerabilities and challenges in providing hyperlocal weather intelligence to smallholder farmers. India’s development and operationalization of BFS mark a significant step in its growing leadership in climate tech and South-South cooperation . The model showcases how locally developed, high-performance systems can support climate resilience and agricultural decision-making across geographies facing shared risks. By contributing such scalable models, India strengthens its role as a global climate solutions provider , supporting other developing nations with proven, adaptable technologies for early warning systems and climate-informed agriculture. A Shift from Imported to Indigenous Intelligence India’s weather forecasting previously leaned on imported models like the Global Forecast System (GFS) and Coupled Forecast System (CFS), both rooted in U.S. technology. BFS breaks this dependence by offering a fully indigenous solution, attuned to Indian and tropical weather complexities. Its development exemplifies India’s technological self-reliance and scientific innovation, making it a flagbearer of Atmanirbhar Bharat in climate science. Climate change is increasing the frequency and unpredictability of extreme events, and having the world’s most accurate operational forecast system could be the difference between catastrophe and resilience for millions. Conclusion: BFS as a Pillar for Viksit Bharat and Global Resilience Marking a major stride in India’s climate innovation journey, the Bharat Forecast System (BFS) exemplifies how indigenous science can shape the future of climate-resilient development. By combining advanced numerical modeling, artificial intelligence, and high-resolution data, BFS stands as a strategic integration of technology and governance aimed at tackling the escalating threats of climate variability. Through hyperlocal, timely, and actionable forecasts, BFS empowers stakeholders across sectors, from farmers and disaster managers to urban planners and public health agencies. It strengthens weekly agro-advisories, enhances real-time decision-making, and supports resource-use efficiency across the farming lifecycle from sowing to harvesting and even market planning. Its applications also extend to smart cities, energy systems, and last-mile warning services. In the broader context, BFS symbolizes India’s commitment to building a Viksit Bharat rooted in data sovereignty and regional resilience. Its adaptability to tropical geographies presents a scalable model for the Global South, paving the way for deeper South-South collaboration in climate-tech and early warning innovations. As India and its peers brace for an era of climate disruption, BFS ensures that weather intelligence is not just technologically superior but also accessible, inclusive, and transformative, ushering in a new paradigm of climate-smart development and grassroots resilience.
